name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q66 - Infeasibility of preparing hydrogen iodide using sulphuric acid

questiontext.text:
Assertion: HI cannot be prepared by the reaction of KI with concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\)
Reason: HI has lowest H–X bond strength among halogen acids.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The laboratory preparation of volatile acids from metal salts depends on the non-volatile nature and oxidising capability of the acid used, as well as the redox stability of the resulting conjugate acid.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
When potassium iodide is treated with concentrated sulphuric acid, hydrogen iodide is initially produced, but concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a moderately strong oxidising agent and immediately oxidises the formed \(\mathrm{HI}\) into elemental iodine (\(\mathrm{I}_2\)), being reduced itself to sulphur dioxide:
\[2\mathrm{KI} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \rightarrow \mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 + \mathrm{I}_2 + \mathrm{SO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]
Consequently, \(\mathrm{HI}\) cannot be prepared using concentrated sulphuric acid (a non-oxidising acid such as \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\) is used instead). Thus, the assertion proposition is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason and Correlation
Descending Group 17, atomic radius increases from fluorine to iodine, leading to longer \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{X}\) internuclear distances and poorer orbital overlap. Consequently, \(\mathrm{HI}\) has the lowest bond dissociation enthalpy and weakest bond strength among the halogen acids (\(\mathrm{HF} > \mathrm{HCl} > \mathrm{HBr} > \mathrm{HI}\)). Thus, the reason proposition is also correct.
However, the underlying reason why \(\mathrm{HI}\) cannot be prepared by this method is the strong oxidising action of concentrated sulphuric acid on hydrogen iodide, not merely the low bond strength of \(\mathrm{HI}\). Therefore, the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, both assertion and reason are correct statements, but reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q67 - Multiple bonding differences between oxygen and sulphur allotropes

questiontext.text:
Assertion: Both rhombic and monoclinic sulphur exist as \(\mathrm{S}_8\) but oxygen exists as \(\mathrm{O}_2\).
Reason: Oxygen forms \(\mathrm{p}\pi - \mathrm{p}\pi\) multiple bond due to small size and small bond length but \(\mathrm{p}\pi - \mathrm{p}\pi\) bonding is not possible in sulphur.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The molecular atomicity of second-period versus third-period elements in Group 16 is governed by the relative stability of multiple \(\mathrm{p}\pi - \mathrm{p}\pi\) bonds compared to single \(\sigma\)-bonds.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Oxygen exists as discrete diatomic molecules (\(\mathrm{O}_2\)) containing a double bond between the oxygen atoms. In contrast, both rhombic (\(\alpha\)) and monoclinic (\(\beta\)) allotropes of sulphur exist as puckered eight-membered crown rings containing eight sulphur atoms linked by single bonds (\(\mathrm{S}_8\)). Thus, the assertion proposition is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason and Correlation
Because of its exceptionally small atomic radius and short bond length, oxygen atoms can approach closely enough to achieve effective sideways overlap of their \(2p\) orbitals, forming strong \(\mathrm{p}\pi - \mathrm{p}\pi\) multiple bonds. In contrast, sulphur atoms have larger atomic radii and diffuse \(3p\) orbitals, which prevents effective lateral overlap, making \(\mathrm{p}\pi - \mathrm{p}\pi\) multiple bonding energetically unfavourable. Instead, sulphur prefers to form catenated single \(\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{S}\) bonds, resulting in the formation of octatomic \(\mathrm{S}_8\) rings. Hence, the reason is correct and directly explains why oxygen is diatomic while sulphur is polyatomic.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, both assertion and reason are correct statements, and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q68 - Oxidation of hydrochloric acid to chlorine gas

questiontext.text:
Assertion: NaCl reacts with concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) to give colourless fumes with pungent smell. But on adding \(\mathrm{MnO}_2\) the fumes become greenish yellow.
Reason: \(\mathrm{MnO}_2\) oxidises HCl to chlorine gas which is greenish yellow.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Volatile acid release followed by oxidative conversion represents a standard qualitative confirmatory sequence for halide salts.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
When sodium chloride reacts with concentrated sulphuric acid, hydrogen chloride gas is produced:
\[\mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \rightarrow \mathrm{NaHSO}_4 + \mathrm{HCl}\uparrow\]
Hydrogen chloride is evolved as colourless, pungent-smelling fumes. Upon the addition of manganese dioxide (\(\mathrm{MnO}_2\)), the evolved fumes turn greenish-yellow. Thus, the assertion proposition is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason and Correlation
Manganese dioxide is an effective oxidising agent in acidic media. It oxidises the generated hydrogen chloride into elemental chlorine gas while being reduced to manganese(II) chloride:
\[\mathrm{MnO}_2 + 4\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnCl}_2 + \mathrm{Cl}_2\uparrow + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]
Chlorine gas has a characteristic greenish-yellow colour and pungent, suffocating odour. This oxidative conversion directly accounts for the colour change of the fumes. Hence, the reason is correct and serves as the correct explanation of the assertion.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, both assertion and reason are correct statements, and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q69 - Kinetic inertness of sulphur hexafluoride towards hydrolysis

questiontext.text:
Assertion: \(\mathrm{SF}_6\) cannot be hydrolysed but \(\mathrm{SF}_4\) can be.
Reason: Six F atoms in \(\mathrm{SF}_6\) prevent the attack of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on sulphur atom of \(\mathrm{SF}_6\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The susceptibility of covalent halides to hydrolysis is controlled by thermodynamic stability, steric access to the central atom, and the presence of vacant coordination sites.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Sulphur hexafluoride (\(\mathrm{SF}_6\)) does not undergo hydrolysis even when heated with steam at high temperatures, exhibiting exceptional chemical inertness. In contrast, sulphur tetrafluoride (\(\mathrm{SF}_4\)) hydrolyses vigorously and smoothly with water to yield sulphur dioxide and hydrogen fluoride:
\[\mathrm{SF}_4 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{SO}_2 + 4\mathrm{HF}\]
Thus, the assertion proposition is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason and Correlation
In \(\mathrm{SF}_6\), the central sulphur atom is in an octahedral coordination geometry surrounded symmetrically by six small fluorine atoms. This creates complete steric crowding (steric hindrance) that physically protects the central sulphur atom, preventing incoming nucleophilic water molecules from attacking. Additionally, sulphur is coordinatively saturated. In \(\mathrm{SF}_4\), the central sulphur atom has a see-saw geometry with only four fluorine atoms and an exposed lone pair, leaving the sulphur atom sterically accessible to nucleophilic attack by water. Hence, the reason is correct and directly explains why \(\mathrm{SF}_6\) resists hydrolysis while \(\mathrm{SF}_4\) does not.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, both assertion and reason are correct statements, and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
